lesson.title: Activation functions: what a neuron does with its sum

objectives.statement: Apply a step, sigmoid, or ReLU function to a given value.
Explain why a network without activation functions can only draw straight lines.
Describe how sigmoid and ReLU differ for large negative and large positive inputs.

segments.title: A sum is not yet an answer

narration.text: In the last lesson a neuron added up its weighted inputs and got a number, z. That number can be anything: large, tiny, or negative.
Before passing it on, the neuron puts z through one more step, called the activation function. It decides how strongly the neuron responds.
Different functions respond in different ways. We will meet three of them.
The simplest is the step function. Below zero it gives zero. At zero or above it gives one. The neuron is either off or on.
The second is called ReLU. Below zero it also gives zero. Above zero it simply passes z through unchanged.
So ReLU of minus three is zero, and ReLU of two is two.

scene.fallback_text: Two graphs side by side. On the left the step function: a flat line at $0$ for negative $z$ that jumps to a flat line at $1$ from $z = 0$ onwards. On the right ReLU: flat at $0$ for negative $z$, then a straight line rising with slope $1$, so that $\mathrm{ReLU}(2) = 2$.

question.stem: A neuron's weighted sum is $z = 2.5$, and it uses ReLU. What is its output?
question.explanation: ReLU is $\max(0, z)$. Since $2.5$ is positive, it passes through unchanged.
question.hint: Is $z$ above or below zero? What does ReLU do in that case?

segments.title: A smooth version of the switch

narration.text: The third function is the sigmoid. It is a smooth version of the step. Slide z and watch the output.
For large negative inputs the output is close to zero. For large positive inputs it is close to one. In between it rises smoothly, and at z equals zero it is exactly one half.

segments.prompt: Slide $z$ from far left to far right. Where does the output change fastest, and where does it hardly change at all?

scene.fallback_text: A graph of the sigmoid function $\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$ for $z$ from $-6$ to $6$: an S-shaped curve that is close to $0$ on the far left, passes through $0.5$ at $z = 0$, and is close to $1$ on the far right. A slider moves a point along the curve, and a number shows the output.

question.stem: For a very large negative input, such as $z = -100$, what do sigmoid and ReLU give?
question.explanation: Sigmoid squeezes every input into the range from $0$ to $1$ and approaches $0$ for large negative inputs. ReLU is $\max(0, z)$, which is $0$ whenever $z$ is negative. The two differ for large positive inputs: sigmoid levels off at $1$, while ReLU keeps growing.
question.hint: Look at the left end of each graph.

options.text: Both give $0$, or very close to it
options.feedback: Yes. Sigmoid flattens out toward $0$, and ReLU is exactly $0$ for every negative input.

options.text: Sigmoid gives about $-1$ and ReLU gives $-100$
options.feedback: Neither function ever gives a negative output. Sigmoid stays between $0$ and $1$, and ReLU replaces negatives with $0$.

options.text: Sigmoid gives about $0$ and ReLU gives $-100$
options.feedback: ReLU passes positive inputs through unchanged, but it replaces every negative input with $0$.
That is what happens at the other end, for large positive inputs, and only for sigmoid.

segments.title: Why not just pass the sum along?

narration.text: You might wonder why a neuron needs any of this. Why not pass the weighted sum straight on?
Here is the trouble. A weighted sum of weighted sums is still just a weighted sum. Stack as many such layers as you like, and the whole network can do no more than a single layer could.
narration.show: Sums of sums are still sums.

narration.text: A network like that can only draw straight lines through its data. An activation function that bends, like ReLU or sigmoid, is what lets a network fit curves.
narration.show: A bend in each neuron lets the network fit curves.

question.stem: Someone builds a network with ten layers but forgets the activation functions, so every neuron passes its weighted sum straight on. What can this network learn?
question.explanation: Each layer computes weighted sums of the layer before. Without an activation function, the output of the whole network is a weighted sum of its inputs, the same kind of thing one layer computes. Depth adds nothing until something that bends sits between the layers.
question.hint: Think about what you get when you take a weighted sum of weighted sums.

options.text: Only what a single layer could: straight-line relationships
options.feedback: Yes. Without a bend anywhere, ten layers collapse into one weighted sum.

options.text: Ten times more than a one-layer network
options.feedback: More layers only help when each one bends its output. Without activation functions the layers collapse into one.
A weighted sum of weighted sums has no bend at all, so not even a gentle curve.

options.text: Nothing at all: it cannot run
options.feedback: It runs, and it can learn straight-line relationships. It just cannot learn anything more.

narration.text: An activation function turns a neuron's weighted sum into its output.
Step switches between zero and one. Sigmoid does the same smoothly. ReLU gives zero for negative inputs and passes positive ones through.
narration.show: Step and sigmoid end at $1$; ReLU keeps growing.

narration.text: Without a function that bends, a deep network is no more capable than a single layer.
Next, we use the step function to make a neuron that decides.

practice.stem: True or false: the step function gives the same output for $z = 0.1$ and for $z = 50$.
practice.explanation: The step function only asks whether $z$ is below zero. Both inputs are above it, so both give $1$.
practice.hint: What is the only thing the step function looks at?

practice.stem: A neuron uses ReLU. Its weighted sum is $z = 3 \times 2 + (-1) \times 8 + 1$. What is its output?
practice.explanation: $z = 6 - 8 + 1 = -1$. ReLU replaces a negative input with $0$, so the output is $0$.
practice.hint: Work out $z$ first. Then ask whether it is negative.

practice.stem: Which of the three functions in this lesson can give an output larger than $1$? Answer with its name.
practice.explanation: Step and sigmoid never go above $1$. ReLU passes positive inputs through unchanged, so $\mathrm{ReLU}(5) = 5$.
practice.hint: Which graph keeps rising as $z$ grows?

practice.stem: Which statement about the sigmoid function is true?
practice.explanation: Sigmoid is a smooth S-shaped curve that approaches $0$ on the left and $1$ on the right without ever reaching either.

options.text: Its output is always between $0$ and $1$
options.feedback: Yes. However large or small the input, sigmoid stays inside that range.

options.text: Its output is exactly $0$ for every negative input
options.feedback: That describes ReLU and the step function. Sigmoid is small but not zero for negative inputs: at $z = -1$ it is about $0.27$.

options.text: Its output keeps growing as the input grows
options.feedback: That describes ReLU. Sigmoid levels off as it approaches $1$.

options.text: Its output jumps straight from $0$ to $1$ at $z = 0$
options.feedback: That describes the step function. Sigmoid rises smoothly and is $0.5$ at $z = 0$.

practice.stem: In your own words: why does a network need activation functions that are not straight lines?
practice.explanation: Depth only helps when something non-linear sits between the layers.

rubric.text: Without them, many layers do no more than one layer could: sums of sums are still sums
A function that bends lets the network fit relationships that are not straight lines

practice.sample_answer: Each layer computes weighted sums. A weighted sum of weighted sums is still a weighted sum, so without a bend the whole network behaves like one layer and can only fit straight-line relationships. An activation that bends, placed between the layers, is what lets depth add something.

scenes.purpose: Show the step function and ReLU side by side.
Let the learner slide an input along the sigmoid curve and read the output.
